power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Is It Time for Teacher Education to Include a Nature-Based Commitment?

text.text: Teacher education increasingly recognises that meaningful outdoor learning depends on teachers' own relationships with nature, yet many enter the profession with limited confidence or formative outdoor experience.

Research shows that children's nature engagement and conservation sensibilities are shaped by the dispositions of the adults who teach them, signalling the need for programmes that nurture teachers' ecological familiarity, interpretive skill and place-based confidence.
However, structural barriers inhibit sustained practice, producing inequitable provision across schools.
Teachers experience tensions between curriculum-driven expectations and the slower, contemplative qualities of outdoor learning, such as dwell time, sensory exploration and unstructured observation.
Inclusive outdoor practice further relies on knowledgeable staff capable of supporting diverse learners.
The role of place, context and culturally shaped nature orientations remains fundamental and requires scrutiny for outdoor learning to move into sustained practice.

Collectively, these insights highlight the need for a systemic, nature-based commitment within teacher education that develops teacher confidence, addresses contextual constraints and expands pedagogical possibilities outdoors.
While the developmental value of nature for children is increasingly recognised, it cannot be assumed that teachers hold positive nature affiliations.

Many teachers enter the profession with limited formative experiences of outdoor environments shaped by cultural, geographical and institutional contexts that may not nurture an easy relationship with natural spaces.

The content within teacher education that links to outdoor or nature experiences requires attention to ensure the situated histories that teachers bring are recognised as child-nature relationships are closely linked with the dispositions and sensibilities of the adults who facilitate them (King et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The content within teacher education that links to outdoor or nature experiences requires attention to ensure the situated histories that teachers bring are recognised as child-nature relationships are closely linked with the dispositions and sensibilities of the adults who facilitate them <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(King et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Outdoor-related skills are tied to the landscapes and communities available to teachers and children and must be nurtured through repeated, meaningful engagement (Price & Barlow, 2024).
text.formatted: Outdoor-related skills are tied to the landscapes and communities available to teachers and children and must be nurtured through repeated, meaningful engagement <ref type="bibr">(Price & Barlow, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Teaching and learning can be place orientated (Harris. 2021), nature based (MacQuarrie, Nugent & Warden. 2015), playful (Mygind et al. 2026) and may involve physical activity and adventurous experiences (Lee, et al 2025).
text.formatted: Teaching and learning can be place orientated <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Harris. 2021)</ref>, nature based (MacQuarrie, Nugent & Warden. 2015), playful <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Mygind et al. 2026</ref>) and may involve physical activity and adventurous experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Lee, et al 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Recognising that teachers need to develop ecological familiarity and placebased confidence is an essential step in embedding outdoor learning within education.

Education has a duty to prepare young people for a climate-affected future through approaches that acknowledge the psychological dimensions of climate change, supporting critical engagement, emotional resilience (Mottishaw & MacQuarrie, 2025), while enabling an appreciation of nature and the outdoors to develop.
text.formatted: Education has a duty to prepare young people for a climate-affected future through approaches that acknowledge the psychological dimensions of climate change, supporting critical engagement, emotional resilience <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Mottishaw & MacQuarrie, 2025)</ref>, while enabling an appreciation of nature and the outdoors to develop.

text.text: This paper sets out a collective argument that emphasises the need for teacher education to explicitly cultivate and support teachers' developing relationships with nature.

There is increasing recognition of the value of nature-based experiences for teachers, although these benefits are marginalised in policy discourse and there is variation in teacher training across different countries (Spencer & Maynard 2015 . Wolf, Kunz & Robin, 2022).
text.formatted: There is increasing recognition of the value of nature-based experiences for teachers, although these benefits are marginalised in policy discourse and there is variation in teacher training across different countries <ref type="bibr">(Spencer & Maynard 2015</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">. Wolf, Kunz & Robin, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Within the UK there is a mixed pattern where enthusiasm for opportunities clash with real-world classrooms as barriers (including resources and training) that were identified across England and Scotland (MacQuarrie. 2018) persist (Prince, Garrett & Ager. 2026) and a contextually driven approach are recognised as valuable to support outdoor and nature experiences.
text.formatted: Within the UK there is a mixed pattern where enthusiasm for opportunities clash with real-world classrooms as barriers (including resources and training) that were identified across England and Scotland (MacQuarrie. 2018) persist <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Prince, Garrett & Ager. 2026</ref>) and a contextually driven approach are recognised as valuable to support outdoor and nature experiences.

text.text: Research emphasises the potential of outdoor experiences for teacher wellbeing, evidencing reductions in psychological fatigue and the reinvigoration of professional energy (Barker, Chisholm, & Foran, 2024).
text.formatted: Research emphasises the potential of outdoor experiences for teacher wellbeing, evidencing reductions in psychological fatigue and the reinvigoration of professional energy <ref type="bibr">(Barker, Chisholm, & Foran, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Yet school grounds are not inherently restorative, particularly when teachers are subject to the same performative demands that structure indoor learning environments (Mason, MacQuarrie & Hennessey, in press).
text.formatted: Yet school grounds are not inherently restorative, particularly when teachers are subject to the same performative demands that structure indoor learning environments <ref type="bibr">(Mason, MacQuarrie & Hennessey, in press</ref>).

text.text: The assumption that outdoor settings automatically nurtures wellbeing warrants caution as the potential restoration that natural spaces may afford are likely constrained by the institutional expectations that shape schools.
Teacher dispositions are also recognised as shaping outdoor practice (Zeni, Schnellert and Brussoni. 2023).
text.formatted: Teacher dispositions are also recognised as shaping outdoor practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Zeni, Schnellert and Brussoni. 2023)</ref>.

text.text: For teachers who infrequently work outside, the confidence exhibited indoors can diminish, fuelling a situational lack of confidence when the predictability of classroom routines diminishes.

Becoming an outdoorexperienced teacher involves personally relevant factors tied to one's professional background, formative childhood encounters with nature and the cultural norms of a school that includes its locality and community (Fraulo, Carrier and Busch. 2025).
text.formatted: Becoming an outdoorexperienced teacher involves personally relevant factors tied to one's professional background, formative childhood encounters with nature and the cultural norms of a school that includes its locality and community <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Fraulo, Carrier and Busch. 2025</ref>).

text.text: Thus, learning outside requires calibrated efforts that are separate to classroom pedagogies.

Teacher education programmes are confronted with a challenge: how to support teachers in building confidence when learning outside while acknowledging the contextual obstacles that may impede their practice.
Teachers committed to outdoor learning emphasise the benefits for students and sharing these insights will be crucial within teacher education (Hennessey, et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Teachers committed to outdoor learning emphasise the benefits for students and sharing these insights will be crucial within teacher education <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Hennessey, et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Engaging in specialist training, such as using fire outdoors, often fuels enthusiasm and collides with difficulties such as lack of adequate shelter or policies that inhibits implementation (MacQuarrie, 2018).
text.formatted: Engaging in specialist training, such as using fire outdoors, often fuels enthusiasm and collides with difficulties such as lack of adequate shelter or policies that inhibits implementation <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(MacQuarrie, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: While specialist training is not always required for teaching outdoors there is considerable variation in outdoor learning across early years and primary provision with outdoor school spaces often noted as requiring improvement (Prince & Diggory, 2024) and barriers to outdoor learning remain persistently influential and impede regular outdoor practice (MacQuarrie, et al. 2015).
text.formatted: While specialist training is not always required for teaching outdoors there is considerable variation in outdoor learning across early years and primary provision with outdoor school spaces often noted as requiring improvement <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Prince & Diggory, 2024)</ref> and barriers to outdoor learning remain persistently influential and impede regular outdoor practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(MacQuarrie, et al. 2015)</ref>.

text.text: While these problems may appear solvable, they require coordination across senior leadership, estates management and teaching staff, making them hard to untangle (Prince, Garrett & Ager. 2026).
text.formatted: While these problems may appear solvable, they require coordination across senior leadership, estates management and teaching staff, making them hard to untangle <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Prince, Garrett & Ager. 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Such pressures intensify when fiscal constraints undermine progress.

Schools recognised for their outdoor learning practice are vulnerable to funding instability, leading to inequitable provision that reflects broader economic, rather than pedagogical, contexts (Hennessey, et al. 2024).
text.formatted: Schools recognised for their outdoor learning practice are vulnerable to funding instability, leading to inequitable provision that reflects broader economic, rather than pedagogical, contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Hennessey, et al. 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Such contradictions reveal a persistent gap between the knowledge teacher education provides and the material realities teachers face where economic circumstance overrides pedagogical commitment.

There is considerable variation in the opportunities to support outdoor oriented pedagogy during initial teacher training (including physical education; Webber, Brymer, & Dillon. 2025) resulting in uneven professional support and differences in trainee teachers' confidence to consider, plan and deliver learning outside of their classroom.
text.formatted: There is considerable variation in the opportunities to support outdoor oriented pedagogy during initial teacher training (including physical education; Webber, Brymer, & Dillon. 2025) resulting in uneven professional support and differences in trainee teachers' confidence to consider, plan and deliver learning outside of their classroom.

text.text: This points to a need for teacher education to address pedagogical development in tandem with school infrastructure, leadership support and related educational realities.

High-quality outdoor experiences for pupils with significant support needs are possible when grounded in UNCRC principles where teachers and teaching assistants work in unison (MacQuarrie, 2018. Atkinson, et. al., 2017).
text.formatted: High-quality outdoor experiences for pupils with significant support needs are possible when grounded in UNCRC principles where teachers and teaching assistants work in unison (MacQuarrie, 2018. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Atkinson, et. al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Optimising experiences for learners with varying requirements requires direct, knowledgeable support.
Without such input, accommodating different needs is dependent on staff expertise and risks perpetuating social inequalities already present across schooling.
Both mainstream and special school settings report struggling to maintain sufficiently knowledgeable staff to meet diverse learner needs outdoors (Hennessey et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Both mainstream and special school settings report struggling to maintain sufficiently knowledgeable staff to meet diverse learner needs outdoors <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Hennessey et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The result is an uneven landscape of provision where the quality of outdoor experiences varies according to staff expertise, resource availability and workload.
Another tension concerns the contemporary expectation that outdoor learning should align with curriculum objectives.
This imperative -to make a convincing case that outdoor experiences visibly "fuel learning"-positions teachers within cultures of performativity where evidence becomes paramount.

Such pressures risk narrowing outdoor pedagogy and overshadow dimensions of outdoor learning, particularly unstructured experiences. Pierce and Beames (2025) note the minimal attention given to unstructured opportunities within their analysis of Irish outdoor education.
text.formatted: Such pressures risk narrowing outdoor pedagogy and overshadow dimensions of outdoor learning, particularly unstructured experiences. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Pierce and Beames (2025)</ref> note the minimal attention given to unstructured opportunities within their analysis of Irish outdoor education.

text.text: Literature on silence offers further insight and reinforces the need to broaden conceptions of learning outdoors. Lees (2012) notes the positive implications of silence for wellbeing, while Su, Wood and Tribe (2023) identify that silence is often characterised by educators as either disengagement or reflective time.
text.formatted: Literature on silence offers further insight and reinforces the need to broaden conceptions of learning outdoors. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Lees (2012)</ref> notes the positive implications of silence for wellbeing, while <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Su, Wood and Tribe (2023)</ref> identify that silence is often characterised by educators as either disengagement or reflective time.

text.text: MacQuarrie and Nugent (2022) similarly identify dwell time (the deliberate practice of slowing down and remaining in one place to observe, notice and experience the environment) as under-recognised within nature-based learning, despite its capacity to deepen children's connection to place. Beames et al. (2023) discussion of curiosity, wonder and "sense spots" reinforces the need for outdoor pedagogies that allow time for lingering, noticing and contemplative engagement.
text.formatted: MacQuarrie and Nugent (2022) similarly identify dwell time (the deliberate practice of slowing down and remaining in one place to observe, notice and experience the environment) as under-recognised within nature-based learning, despite its capacity to deepen children's connection to place. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Beames et al. (2023)</ref> discussion of curiosity, wonder and "sense spots" reinforces the need for outdoor pedagogies that allow time for lingering, noticing and contemplative engagement.

text.text: These insights provide fertile ground for teacher education to articulate richer pedagogical possibilities outdoors; where outdoor learning should encompass activity as well as recognising the value of pacing, attentiveness and the capacity to allow children (and teachers) to linger.
It remains to be seen to what extent these dimensions feature in teacher education programmes, even if they are essential to cultivating the climate suited to sustaining learning outside.
If outdoor learning is to become a sustained and equitable feature of schooling, teacher education must embed a more intentional nature-based commitment.

This commitment would acknowledge teachers' nature dispositions are varied, contextual constraints shape provision and the pedagogical value of slow, attentive engagement with nature requires a skilled teacher.

It would address structural barriers, recognise the importance of inclusion and staff expertise and prepare teachers to navigate the tensions between curriculum demands and the slower, sensory, relational qualities of outdoor experience (dimensions often marginalised within curriculum-driven cultures).

Most importantly, it would make it easier at every stage of teacher education for teachers to develop the confidence, inspiration and pedagogical grounding needed to foster meaningful outdoor learning for every child ensuring equitable access.
Without such grounding, outdoor learning risks remaining uneven, fragile and overly dependent on the enthusiasm of individual teachers.
A naturebased concordat within teacher education offers a pathway toward meaningful, sustainable and equitable outdoor experiences for all learners and their teachers.
